name: Langflow
description: Visual tool for building and deploying AI agents and workflows
scored_configuration: Local `uv pip install langflow` + `langflow run` with shipped defaults: localhost:7860, allow_custom_components=true, sandbox_backend=none, agentic_experience (Assistant) on, MCP auto-init on, telemetry on.
headline: Run as the README shows, Langflow's default authentication is not locked down. Flows, agent tools, custom components and the built-in Assistant's generated code all run inside the server process, which holds every stored credential and the key that decrypts them. Defenses against server-side request forgery (SSRF) and file-path restriction are good and on by default. A microVM sandbox and per-tool human approval exist, but both are opt-in, and nothing limits what a prompt-injected agent can do with its tools.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: Started the way the README says (`langflow run`), default authentication is not locked down. Every flow, agent and custom component runs inside the server process with that process's full authority, including the database and the key that decrypts every user's stored credentials. The HTTP API checks that a user owns a flow, but the role-based authorization layer is off by default and needs a plugin.

S.finding: The default identity is not locked down, and component code runs with the server process's ambient authority over the DB, the secret key and the environment.
S.gap: No dedicated, narrowly scoped identity for flow/agent execution; L1 needs at least a separate identity for running agents.

C.finding: Flow APIs apply an owner check (owner override, then optional plugin), and MCP stdio subprocesses get a scrubbed env, but in-process components and code reach credentials and the DB directly.
C.gap: In-process components and custom code bypass the authorization layer; L2 needs every built-in tool to act through the scoped identity.

evidence.contains: Check flow permission (owner override, then plugin enforce).

D.finding: Default authentication is not locked down.
D.gap: L1 needs a narrower default identity.

B.finding: A hijacked flow or escaped code runs in the process that holds every user's encrypted credentials and the Fernet key that decrypts them.
B.gap: Credentials for all users and services are reachable from the execution process; L1 needs blast radius limited below cross-tenant/all-service access.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: The Agent component has a per-tool human approval step: a reviewer can approve, edit or reject a pending tool call from the UI, and an authenticated flow-execute permission check guards the resume endpoint. It is off by default: a tool is gated only if the flow author picks approval actions for it, and none are picked by default. Nothing gates components that run directly in a flow, and nothing gates the built-in Assistant, which runs model-generated component code in-process to validate it. Assistant edits to a flow get a restore point, but external actions have no undo.

cap.reason: The Assistant's runtime validation executes model-generated component code in-process without any approval gate, on by default.

S.finding: When enabled, LangChain HumanInTheLoopMiddleware pauses the agent and the card shows the middleware's action description (tool name and args per the library default), with approve/edit/reject.
S.gap: No risk tiers or argument-level policy, and the card shows only the first action's description; L3 needs per-call display of every exact call with risk tiers.

C.finding: Only agent tools whose metadata carries approval_actions are gated; direct component execution and the Assistant's code-running path never cross the gate.
C.gap: Unflagged tools and non-agent paths bypass; L2 needs all built-in tools gated.

D.finding: approval_actions is empty unless the flow author selects actions per tool, so approval is opt-in.
D.gap: Approval is opt-in; L1 needs approval on by default for consequential tools.

B.finding: Assistant canvas edits get a flow-version restore point; API requests, messages and code execution are irreversible.
B.gap: External actions (HTTP writes, messages, code) have no undo; L2 needs reversibility for the common case.

evidence.contains: Assistant restore points built on the existing flow-versioning system.

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: The built-in network and file components are well validated. URL, API Request and Web Search block internal and cloud-metadata addresses, pin DNS, and re-validate each redirect. File components resolve paths and keep them inside the user's storage directory. Both protections are on by default. But the toolbox also has general-purpose tools, such as the Python Interpreter, raw HTTP to any public host, custom component code and whole MCP servers, and there is no central policy layer that every tool inherits.

S.finding: Strong allowlist-style checks exist (SSRF IP blocking with DNS pinning and per-hop redirect validation; resolved-path containment), but general tools such as the Python Interpreter and arbitrary-method HTTP stay largely passthrough.
S.gap: General-purpose tools (code, any public URL/method) remain the default building blocks; L3 needs allowlist validation on every tool's arguments.

C.finding: SSRF and path checks are applied per built-in component; MCP tools and custom components get no shared validation layer.
C.gap: No shared validation layer for MCP and custom components; L3 needs extension tools wrapped by a shared layer.

D.finding: The Agent has no tools until a flow author wires them, but the on-by-default Assistant ships with build/run/generate tools, and an MCP Tools node exposes a server's whole tool set.
D.gap: Write/exec tools are routinely wired, with no read-only default set; L3 needs a read-only default with explicit enabling of write/exec.

B.finding: A misused tool reaches any public host and in-process code execution; only internal addresses and out-of-storage file paths are blocked.
B.gap: Reach is server-wide with only minor limits; L2 needs tools scoped to a project/workspace.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: By default, model-written Python (the Python Interpreter tool, Smart Transform) runs inside the Langflow server process. The only protection is restricted builtins and AST checks, which the maintainers describe as best-effort and not a guaranteed sandbox. Custom component code, and the Assistant's validation of model-generated components, also run in-process, and MCP stdio servers start on the host. An escape lands in the process that holds the database, the secret key and every stored credential. An optional QEMU microVM backend (exec-sandbox) with no network and fail-closed behaviour exists, but it is off by default and covers only the Python Interpreter and REPL components.

cap.reason: Opt-in mechanism: off in the scored default configuration.

S.finding: Each execution runs in a dedicated QEMU microVM with a read-only rootfs and no host filesystem; software emulation is refused by default.

evidence.contains: each execution runs in a dedicated QEMU microVM

C.finding: Only the Python Interpreter and legacy REPL route to the sandbox; custom components, Smart Transform, Assistant validation and MCP stdio stay in-process or on the host.
C.gap: Other execution paths stay on the host; L2 needs most paths sandboxed.

evidence.contains: Execution backend for user-authored code in the code-execution components

D.finding: sandbox_backend defaults to 'none'.
D.gap: Off by default; L1 needs the sandbox on by default.

B.finding: No network by default, memory and timeout limits, no host filesystem, and fail-closed when unavailable.
B.gap: Per-call ephemerality is not verified in Langflow's code (upstream warm pool); L4 needs ephemeral, verified per-run VMs.

evidence.contains: fails closed with an error instead of silently running in-process

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: Nothing structural limits what a hijacked agent can do. Web pages, files, search results and MCP tool output come back as ordinary tool messages. The only defence is a line in the default system prompt telling the model to treat tool output as untrusted. One agent can read attacker-controlled content, hold stored credentials, and send data to any public host or take irreversible actions, all without a human.

cap.reason: Worst case (B L0): a hijacked agent can leak data and take irreversible actions unattended.

S.finding: The only injection defence is a system-prompt instruction; there is no taint tracking or quarantine.
S.gap: Prompt-only; L1 needs at least a detection layer on by default.

evidence.note: 2 hits are system-prompt text, 2 are A2A card coercion; none gate tools on provenance.

C.finding: Tool results, MCP output and fetched pages enter context with the same standing as user input.
C.gap: Untrusted sources are not distinguished; L1 needs at least one source handled.

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: Agent chat history is stored per session and fed back as conversation (up to 100 messages by default) with no validation, so injected text persists for as long as a session id is reused. Queries scope history by session, flow and user. The Assistant also saves model-generated component code to disk after scanning it, and later turns import and execute that code. Vector stores and knowledge bases written by flows have no provenance tagging.
criteria.notes: The `langflow` entry point calls load_dotenv() at import (src/backend/base/langflow/langflow_launcher.py:6-8). Langflow is a server, not an agent working inside a cloned repository, so this was treated as operator scope and C6-REPOCONFIG was not applied.

S.finding: Chat history writes are not validated and are re-injected as conversation; only the Assistant's generated-component store has a (denylist) scan.
S.gap: No provenance labelling or validation of persisted memory; L2 needs memory presented as data with provenance.

C.finding: The generated-component registry is scanned; chat history, vector stores and knowledge bases are not controlled.
C.gap: Most stores uncontrolled; L2 needs the main memory store controlled.

criteria.name: Third-party extensions
criteria.question: Are plugins, MCP servers and downloaded tools verified or isolated before they run with the agent's access?
criteria.summary: On startup, Langflow adds an MCP server entry for each user's starter project. The entry runs `uvx mcp-proxy` with no version pin, so whatever release PyPI serves is downloaded and run when the server is checked or used. Users can add more stdio servers through npx/uvx/docker. A command allowlist, a shell-metacharacter policy and an environment-variable denylist apply, but versions are not pinned and nothing checks integrity. The package allowlist and the interpreter and Docker hardening are opt-in. Stdio servers start with a scrubbed environment (PATH plus their own config), but they run as the same OS user.

cap.reason: By default Langflow configures, and launches when the server is listed or used, an unpinned `uvx mcp-proxy` from PyPI, executing remote code without user consent.

S.finding: Auto-configured `uvx mcp-proxy` resolves the latest PyPI release; user-added npx/uvx servers are unpinned with no hash check.
S.gap: Third-party packages run unpinned and unverified; L1 needs user-chosen sources only, with nothing auto-installed.

evidence.note: The single hit is the PYTHONHASHSEED env-var name in a denylist, not an integrity check.

C.finding: No extension type has version or integrity verification by default.
C.gap: No extension type is verified; L1 needs at least one.

D.finding: Startup reconciliation auto-adds the mcp-proxy server entry for every user's starter project without consent.
D.gap: Extensions are enabled automatically; L1 needs install on first use behind consent.

evidence.contains: can spawn ``uvx mcp-proxy`` and open an outbound connection

B.gap: No per-extension sandbox or scoped credentials; L3 needs per-extension sandboxing.

criteria.name: Secrets & sensitive-data protection
criteria.question: Are credentials and sensitive data kept out of logs, telemetry, subprocesses, and the model provider?
criteria.summary: Credential-type variables are Fernet-encrypted in the database. The key sits in a permission-restricted file in the same config directory, so anyone who can read that directory can decrypt them. Settings use SecretStr. Transaction logs mask values under sensitive key names, and telemetry sends only allowlisted input fields. Usage telemetry to Scarf is on by default and includes error messages. Nothing redacts secrets before model-bound messages. Provider keys are long-lived, and in-process code can reach them.

S.finding: Fernet encryption at rest for credential variables with a co-located key file, SecretStr settings, and key-name masking in transactions.
S.gap: No OS keychain or secret manager, and no redaction before model-bound messages; L3 needs both.

C.finding: Transaction logs and stored vertex data are masked by key name, and MCP subprocess env is scrubbed, but model-bound messages and telemetry error strings are not redacted.
C.gap: Model-bound messages and telemetry not covered; L3 needs all listed paths.

D.finding: Telemetry is on unless DO_NOT_TRACK is set; payloads are mostly content-free (allowlisted input fields) but include error messages.
D.gap: Telemetry is on by default; L2 needs it opt-in.

evidence.contains: track_in_telemetry: CoalesceBool = False  # Never track secret inputs

B.gap: Long-lived keys; L2 needs scoped keys.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: Every component run is written to a transactions table with inputs, outputs, status and timestamp. Agent tool calls are kept in stored messages as tool-use content blocks with name, input and output. Records lack an actor or approver field, and the authorization audit log is off by default. Writes go through a best-effort background writer that drops rows on a hard crash. Retention keeps only the newest 3,000 transactions, and the server process, where flows and code run, can alter the records.

S.finding: Structured per-component transaction rows and per-tool-call content blocks (name, input, output, error).
S.gap: No actor, approver or delegation attribution on records; L3 needs principal/approver fields and correlation IDs.

C.finding: Every component execution and agent tool call (including MCP tools wired to the agent) is recorded, but approvals and denials are not in the same record, and authz audit is opt-in.
C.gap: Approvals and denials not consistently captured; L3 needs them recorded.

D.finding: On by default in the server DB outside any workspace, but writable by the same process that runs flows and code; retention prunes old rows.
D.gap: The executing process can alter or delete records; L3 needs a writer the model cannot control.

B.finding: Best-effort batched background writer; hard kills lose buffered rows and the queue drops the oldest rows under pressure.
B.gap: Records are flushed late and can be lost; L2 needs per-action flush with surfaced errors.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: The Agent is capped at 15 model calls by default, enforced by middleware. MCP tool calls time out after 180 seconds, and synchronous v2 workflow runs after 300. There is no token or cost budget. Background jobs have no timeout by default. Sub-flows and agents used as tools start with their own fresh limits. Cancelling a build cancels the asyncio task, but in-process code already running is not interrupted.

S.finding: Iteration cap via ModelCallLimitMiddleware plus MCP tool and sync-workflow wall-clock timeouts.
S.gap: No token/cost cap or rate limits on side-effecting tools; L3 needs both.

evidence.note: No token or cost budget in the agent loop.

C.finding: Top-level agent loop plus tool timeouts; sub-flows and background jobs run with their own budgets.
C.gap: Sub-agents and background jobs do not share the parent budget; L3 needs them counted against it.

D.finding: Sensible default of 15 iterations, operator/flow-author configurable up to 128000.
D.gap: Delegating to a sub-flow or agent-as-tool resets the budget; L3 needs limits that delegation cannot reset.

B.finding: Background jobs are unbounded by default, and a cancel stops the task loop but cannot interrupt in-process exec already running.
B.gap: Unbounded background work and non-interruptible execution; L2 needs moderate ceilings for every run.

critical_findings.summary: Startup auto-configures an unpinned `uvx mcp-proxy` MCP server per user, which runs the latest PyPI release without consent.

rule_of_two.untrusted_input: URL / Web Search / File / MCP tool output enters agent context (src/lfx/src/lfx/components/data_source/url.py:287)
rule_of_two.sensitive_data: Encrypted credential variables decrypted into components in the same process (src/backend/base/langflow/services/variable/service.py:661)
rule_of_two.state_change_or_egress: API Request to any public host and code execution tools (src/lfx/src/lfx/components/data_source/api_request.py:546)

fixes.summary: Pin mcp-proxy to an exact version (as mcp-composer already is) and require consent before auto-adding MCP servers.
Pre-select approval actions for code-execution and non-GET HTTP tools so the agent pauses for a human by default.
Route every code-execution path (custom components, Smart Transform, Assistant validation) through the exec-sandbox backend when configured.
Set a default background_job_timeout and make sub-flows/agents-as-tools share the parent's iteration budget.

limitations: Static source review of the pinned commit only; nothing was executed, installed, or probed.
No release tag points at the pinned commit; pyproject.toml declares version 1.12.4.
Scored the README-led local install (`langflow run`). The official Docker image differs in its authentication and user defaults (docker/build_and_push.Dockerfile:231-237), which would improve C1.
LangChain HumanInTheLoopMiddleware behaviour (which arguments the approval description contains) and exec-sandbox upstream VM lifecycle were inferred from library contracts, not read in their source.

Not examined in depth: the frontend's markdown rendering as an exfiltration channel, the src/bundles provider packages, enterprise authorization plugins, Langflow Desktop, and the A2A/public-flow serving plane (opt-in features).
No text aimed at AI reviewers was found in AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or other markdown files.
